articles.title: Service Changes on Rochdale Line Due to Planned Works
articles.excerpt: Planned works on the Rochdale line will result in service changes from 15 to 28 August, with bus replacements in place for affected stops.
articles.content_html:
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has announced that planned works will take place on the Rochdale line from Saturday 15 August until Friday 28 August, resulting in significant service changes. During this period, a bus replacement service will operate between affected stops to accommodate passengers.

Additionally, on Saturday 15 and Sunday 16 August, works will occur in Manchester city centre, specifically at Manchester Town Hall. Consequently, no trams will operate via Exchange Square, with services on the East Didsbury and Trafford Centre lines rerouted via Market Street and Shudehill instead.

Passengers are advised to plan their journeys accordingly, as these disruptions may affect travel times. TfGM encourages those needing assistance or further information to contact their customer service help point or call the Metrolink contact centre at 0161 244 1000, available from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

In addition to the Rochdale line works, essential improvement works will take place at Prestwich Metrolink stop from Monday 18 May to Wednesday 19 August. While tram services will not be affected, an increased presence of staff is expected at this stop during this time.

articles.title: LIVE: GMP student officer arrested on suspicion of rape and kidnap after M62 pursuit
articles.excerpt: LIVE updates after a 23-year-old Greater Manchester Police student officer was arrested on suspicion of rape, kidnap and dangerous driving following a pursuit on the M62.
articles.content_html:
LIVE UPDATES — This story is being updated as further confirmed information becomes available.

18:50 — Greater Manchester Police says it is committed to working with the Crown Prosecution Service to bring the case to court as quickly as possible, while also accelerating misconduct proceedings within police regulations. Assistant Chief Constable Mark Dexter said the allegations were deeply concerning and disturbing and said all necessary and decisive action would be taken in the interests of the woman and the public.

GMP has confirmed its Professional Standards Directorate carried out an initial review of the officer's vetting and found it had been completed without any reason for concern. The force stressed that this did not lessen the severity of the allegations.

18:42 — Rochdale Daily moved this breaking story to live coverage. We will add confirmed developments from Greater Manchester Police, the Independent Office for Police Conduct and other authoritative sources as they emerge.

WHAT WE KNOW SO FAR

A 23-year-old Greater Manchester Police student officer has been arrested on suspicion of rape and kidnap following a police pursuit on the M62.

The officer was off duty when a 999 call was received shortly before 10.20pm on Saturday. Police said a woman in her 20s could be heard in distress in a vehicle in the Manchester area.

Officers traced the suspect's personal vehicle and began a pursuit. The pursuit continued onto the M62 before the officer was detained in West Yorkshire.

The 23-year-old was arrested on suspicion of rape, kidnap and dangerous driving. GMP says he has been suspended from duty and remains in custody for questioning.

The woman is being supported by specialist officers and other agencies.

Greater Manchester Police has made a voluntary referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct. Internal misconduct proceedings are also being progressed.

Assistant Chief Constable Mark Dexter said thousands of GMP officers and staff who work to protect the public would be shocked and angered by the allegations. He said specialist resources had been assigned to the investigation and gave a commitment that the force would work with prosecutors as the criminal investigation progresses.

The allegations have not been proven. An arrest does not amount to a finding of guilt and the officer is entitled to the presumption of innocence unless and until convicted. This live page will be updated when further information is confirmed.
articles.legal_disclaimer: No finding of guilt should be inferred from an arrest, allegation or charge. Anyone accused is presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

articles.title: New Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig visits Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Newly elected Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today as she begins work across the city-region following her victory in last month's mayoral by-election.
articles.content_html:
Newly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today, bringing the new city-region mayor to the borough during the opening days of her term.

Craig was elected at the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election on 30 July, succeeding Andy Burnham after his return to Westminster. She became the first woman to hold the Greater Manchester mayoralty.

The visit puts Rochdale among the places receiving early attention from the new mayor as she begins the job of representing all ten Greater Manchester boroughs.

At the time of publication, no detailed public itinerary or standalone press release about today's Rochdale visit had been published on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority news pages. Rochdale Daily has checked publicly available material from the mayoral and GMCA press operation and will update this article if further details, photographs or statements are released.

Craig arrives in Rochdale having campaigned on a platform that included expanding the Bee Network, freezing bus fares and extending free bus travel to young people aged 11 to 18. She has also placed housing, economic growth and reducing inequalities among the central issues facing Greater Manchester.

Those priorities are particularly relevant to Rochdale, where transport connectivity, town-centre investment, housing and access to opportunity remain major local issues.

Before becoming mayor, Craig led Manchester City Council from December 2021 and held Greater Manchester responsibilities for economy, business and inclusive growth. She was awarded an OBE in March 2026 for services to local government.

Her election followed the departure of Andy Burnham from the mayoralty. Craig won the contest after the count proceeded to a second round, defeating Reform UK's Sian Astley.

Today's Rochdale visit will therefore be watched for signs of how the new mayor intends to translate her city-region promises into action for individual boroughs outside Manchester city centre.

Rochdale Daily will add any confirmed detail released by the mayor's press team about the purpose of the visit, people she met or commitments made while in the borough.

articles.title: £12m plan aims to bring Storage World Middleton site back to life after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: A £12m rebirth bid has been launched for the Storage World site in Middleton, more than a year after a devastating fire destroyed the Old Hall Street facility.
articles.content_html:
A £12m bid to bring the Storage World site in Middleton back to life has been launched, marking a major potential investment in an important part of the town centre following last year's devastating fire.

The proposals concern the Storage World site on Old Hall Street, next to Middleton Arena. The former storage facility was badly damaged by a major blaze in June 2025, which burned for several days and led to demolition of the building. No injuries were reported, although customers and businesses suffered significant losses.

Place North West has reported that Storage World has now launched a £12m rebirth bid for the site. The move comes as regeneration work and planning for the wider Middleton town centre area continues.

Official Rochdale Development Agency updates show that the council and RDA have remained in discussions with Storage World since the fire. In June, the RDA said it was working with stakeholders to develop key principles for the area, including the potential to deliver improvements to Middleton Arena and create a new public space. It also confirmed that discussions with Storage World were continuing with input from Rochdale Borough Council's planning team.

The site is particularly significant because of its position beside Middleton Arena and within an area being considered as part of wider plans for the future of Middleton town centre. Earlier council reports said the outcomes of discussions over Storage World and the arena would feed into wider masterplanning work.

Before the fire, Storage World operated a large self-storage and workspace facility from Old Hall Street. The Middleton operation had previously expanded as demand grew, with the company providing traditional storage alongside space used by small and online businesses.

The 2025 blaze had a substantial impact on customers. Fire crews worked for days at the scene and parts of the building were demolished while firefighting operations were still under way to allow crews safe access. Storage World said at the time that its team was devastated by the impact on customers and the wider community.

The latest £12m proposal therefore represents a potentially significant next chapter for a prominent town-centre site and comes at a time when Middleton is the subject of wider regeneration and masterplanning proposals.

Rochdale Daily will update this story as further planning documents and details of the proposed redevelopment become publicly available.

articles.title: Wildfire emergency alert: an overreaction, or a sign of things to come?
articles.excerpt: Millions of phones across England and Wales sounded a Government Emergency Alert as wildfire risk reached exceptional levels. Was the intrusive warning proportionate, or are Britons being introduced to a hazard we will increasingly have to live with?
articles.content_html:
Millions of mobile phones across England and Wales emitted the unmistakable siren of the Government's Emergency Alerts system on Friday evening, carrying a warning about the risk of wildfires during exceptionally hot and dry conditions. People were urged not to light barbecues, campfires, bonfires or fireworks and to call 999 if they saw a fire.

For many people in Rochdale, where there was no wall of flame approaching their homes and no instruction to evacuate, the reaction was understandable: was this really what the country's most intrusive public-warning system was designed for? Emergency Alerts override ordinary phone settings and make a deliberately alarming noise intended to make people stop what they are doing immediately. Until recently, many people probably imagined receiving one only where there was a direct and imminent threat to life.

That makes the question worth asking. Was Friday's warning an overreaction, or was it an indication of how Britain's relationship with extreme weather is changing?

There is a reasonable argument that the Government must be careful not to overuse the system. Emergency warnings derive much of their effectiveness from their rarity. If people become accustomed to the siren being used for preventative advice that could have been distributed through television, radio, ordinary text messages and social media, warning fatigue becomes a real concern. A person who concludes that the alerts are unnecessarily dramatic may disable them and then miss a genuinely local warning about rapidly rising floodwater, an industrial accident or a fire approaching their home.

The Government should therefore be prepared to explain why this particular threshold was met and why an alert covering England and Wales was considered preferable to narrower regional warnings. Public confidence in an emergency system depends partly upon people understanding why its most intrusive warning mechanism has been activated.

However, dismissing the warning as hysteria would ignore the extraordinary situation confronting fire and rescue services this summer. Britain has experienced a succession of major wildfires during prolonged heat and drought. By Friday, national reporting indicated that the number of wildfires in England and Wales had already exceeded the 1,017 recorded during 2025, itself a record year. Dozens of fires were active around the country, major incidents had been declared, homes had been destroyed in the West Midlands and military personnel were being deployed to assist overstretched emergency services.

That changes the context considerably. Friday's message was not sent because somebody in Whitehall had suddenly discovered that dry grass can burn. It arrived during an active national wildfire emergency in which firefighters were already dealing with the consequences of repeated ignition in exceptionally dry landscapes.

The important distinction is between the probability of a fire starting and the severity of what may happen once one starts. Fire-danger measures do not necessarily predict that a particular patch of moorland will ignite. They indicate how easily vegetation may burn and how difficult a fire could become to control if ignition occurs. During ordinary British weather, carelessly discarded heat may produce a small scorched area. During prolonged heat, low humidity and very dry vegetation, the same ignition can develop into a fire requiring numerous appliances and many hours of firefighting.

Human behaviour therefore matters enormously. The Government cannot immediately cool the country, restore moisture to dried vegetation or remove weeks of accumulated heat from the landscape. It can, however, try to reduce avoidable sources of ignition. Disposable barbecues, bonfires, campfires, cigarettes, fireworks and other sources of heat can become much more consequential when the surrounding vegetation has effectively become fuel.

There is also a longer-term reason for taking the warning seriously. Britain is not becoming Spain, Greece or California overnight, and comparisons with those places can easily become exaggerated. Our climate, vegetation, housing patterns and emergency infrastructure are different. Nevertheless, the assumption that serious wildfire is an exotic problem belonging somewhere else is increasingly difficult to defend.

The UK has already experienced destructive moorland fires during previous hot summers, including the extensive Saddleworth Moor fires of 2018. For Rochdale this is not an abstract national concern. Moorland, grassland and countryside sit immediately beside settlements across the Pennine fringe, including areas around Littleborough, Wardle, Norden, Whitworth and the wider hills surrounding the borough. A serious moorland fire does not need to reach Rochdale town centre to affect Rochdale residents. Smoke, road closures, damaged habitats, exhausted emergency-service resources and threats to isolated properties can all spread consequences far beyond the flames themselves.

Climate science also points towards a future in which the weather conditions favourable to wildfire become more common. Research involving the Met Office and UK scientific institutions has concluded that human-caused climate change substantially increased the likelihood of the severe fire weather experienced during the 2022 heatwave. Climate-risk assessments anticipate more high fire-weather days as average temperatures rise, while longer periods of heat and drought can leave vegetation increasingly vulnerable to ignition.

That does not mean climate change can be blamed automatically for every individual fire. Fires still require ignition, fuel and conditions that allow them to spread. Land management, deliberate arson, accidental ignition and the speed of the emergency response all remain important. But the broader direction is difficult to ignore: a warmer climate can create more frequent periods in which an otherwise minor act of carelessness has much larger consequences.

This is why there is a sensible position between panic and dismissal. The Government should not turn the Emergency Alerts system into an electronic public-information poster. If the siren sounds too often for advice that is not genuinely urgent, its effectiveness may be weakened. Equally, a warning designed to prevent new fires during an already exceptional national wildfire situation is not obviously frivolous simply because no flames were visible from the recipient's window.

In fact, prevention may be one of the strongest arguments for using the system. Waiting until a wildfire is already moving towards houses means waiting until much of the opportunity to stop the emergency has disappeared. If a short national warning prevents even a small number of avoidable ignitions at a time when firefighters are already stretched, the intervention may prove proportionate despite its dramatic presentation.

The most interesting aspect of Friday's alert is therefore not the ten seconds of noise. It is what the noise was about. Britain has spent generations regarding wildfire principally as a rural inconvenience or an overseas catastrophe. Emergency planners are now treating it as a hazard capable of threatening homes, infrastructure and life on a sufficiently large scale to justify use of a national warning system.

For residents of Rochdale and the wider Pennine area, that deserves attention. Our landscape contains precisely the combination of moorland, grass, woodland and settlements that can make prolonged dry conditions problematic. The lesson is not that every warm weekend should cause millions of phones to scream. It is that the range of emergencies Britain prepares for may be changing.

If wetter summers return and warnings of this kind remain extremely rare, Friday's alert may ultimately be remembered as an unusually cautious intervention during an exceptional season. If periods of intense heat, drought and severe fire weather become more frequent, it may instead look like an early example of something the public later comes to regard as normal.

That is the uncomfortable possibility behind the alarm. The argument is not really about whether people were irritated by their phones. It is about whether Britain is entering a period in which hazards once considered unusual have to become part of ordinary civil protection.

Whether Friday's alert was perfectly calibrated is open to debate. The underlying wildfire risk is not.

articles.title: URGENT: Police appeal to find missing 10-year-old Rayah in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police has launched an urgent appeal to find 10-year-old Rayah, who was last seen on Bower Avenue in Rochdale at around 8.30am today.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester Police has launched an urgent appeal to find 10-year-old Rayah, who has been missing from Rochdale since this morning.

Rayah was last seen on Bower Avenue in Rochdale at around 8.30am on Friday 14 August. Police say officers are becoming increasingly concerned about her and want to make sure she is safe and well.

The police appeal describes Rayah as a child with olive or tanned skin, approximately 4ft 5in tall, with mousey brown curly hair worn in a ponytail.

She was last seen wearing purple and white striped bottoms, a T-shirt and a denim jacket. She was also carrying a backpack and had a remote-control car with her.

Anyone who sees Rayah, knows where she may be, or has information which could help officers locate her is urged to contact Greater Manchester Police on 0161 856 1367, quoting reference MSP/06PP/0001322/26.

Always call 999 in an emergency.

Rochdale Daily will update this appeal as soon as further verified information is released by police.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Netball launched as Rochdale Netball Club joins Dale family
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Netball Club is becoming Rochdale AFC Netball in a new partnership with Rochdale AFC and its Community Trust, bringing nearly 200 weekly players into the club's wider sporting family.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Netball Club is joining the Rochdale AFC family under a new identity as Rochdale AFC Netball, in a partnership designed to grow the sport and create more opportunities for women, girls and the wider community across the borough.

The agreement brings together Rochdale AFC, Rochdale AFC Community Trust and one of the borough's established community sports clubs under the wider 'Our Teams' banner.

Rochdale Netball Club currently runs teams from under-six level through to seniors, with nearly 200 players taking to the court each week. Under the new Rochdale AFC Netball identity, the organisations hope to strengthen the route from school participation into junior and adult club netball while also expanding opportunities in coaching, volunteering and leadership.

The partnership is expected to support new programmes in schools, holiday provision, health and wellbeing and volunteer development. The shared Rochdale AFC identity could also open up additional opportunities for sponsorship, commercial support, community events and promotion through the football club.

Amy Williams, Chair of Rochdale AFC Netball, described the move as a fantastic opportunity for both the club and the sport locally, saying joining the Rochdale AFC family would provide a stronger platform to grow the game and inspire more women and girls to become involved.

Rochdale AFC chief executive Laura Thomas, herself a former netball player, said she was thrilled to welcome the club into the wider Rochdale AFC family and stressed that the club's ambition to build a thriving community extends beyond football.

Ryan Bradley, Community Director at Rochdale AFC Community Trust, said the football club, charity and netball club shared common values and could combine their respective strengths. He said bringing the organisations together under one brand would raise netball's profile in Rochdale and strengthen support for volunteers, coaches, community outreach and school work.

Rochdale AFC Netball will be based at Edgar Wood. The Community Trust also pointed to plans for the Community Football and Wellbeing Hub at Bowlee, saying the geographical proximity of the projects made closer cooperation a natural step.

The move follows a wider trend in British sport in which professional football and rugby clubs have partnered with netball organisations to increase visibility, participation and long-term sustainability. In Rochdale, the organisations say their approach will remain community focused and open to people of all ages.

Further information about Rochdale AFC Netball teams, programmes and opportunities to get involved is expected to be announced in due course.

articles.title: Homelessness, addiction and the cruelty of public condemnation
articles.excerpt: A disabled homeless man outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road has become the subject of photographs, insults and jokes online. The harder question is whether public humiliation solves anything at all.
articles.content_html:
There is a homeless man who regularly sits outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road in Rochdale. He uses a wheelchair, has one leg, and appears to have longstanding problems with drug dependency. In recent days, photographs purporting to show him using drugs have been circulated in a local social-media group, accompanied by descriptions including ‘junkie’, ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’, together with jokes about his disability.

Those comments deserve more scrutiny than the man they were aimed at.

It is entirely legitimate for residents to object to public drug use, theft, abusive behaviour or intimidation. It is legitimate for shop workers to expect protection at work. It is legitimate for parents to dislike exposing children to distressing scenes. But there is a clear moral distinction between criticising behaviour and publicly degrading a vulnerable person. Calling a homeless, disabled man a ‘scruff’ does not protect children. Making jokes about his missing leg does not reduce drug use. Posting photographs of him at what may be one of the lowest points of his life does not help shop staff, improve public safety or increase the likelihood that he enters treatment. It serves a different purpose: humiliation.

The ease with which some people have participated in that humiliation should trouble us.

The editor of Rochdale Daily has spoken to this man several times. In those encounters, he has not demanded money. He has generally asked for a drink, usually a chocolate milkshake. Other residents have independently described similar experiences. A Tesco worker has, by contrast, said that staff sometimes experience him as abusive. Both accounts may be true. Addiction, withdrawal, mental distress and homelessness do not produce consistent behaviour.

That does not make abuse acceptable. But neither does difficult behaviour grant the public permission to strip somebody of dignity.

During one conversation, the man said he had previously been prescribed methadone but stopped collecting it because he felt demeaned and discriminated against when attending the dispensing pharmacy. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that account. When asked whether he would consider restarting treatment if his medication could be dispensed somewhere he felt able to attend, he said yes.

That exchange should matter more than a photograph. It suggests that beneath the visible disorder is a person who can still discuss treatment, medication and the possibility of changing his circumstances. Yet this is precisely the sort of person whom public discussion can rapidly reduce to a caricature. Once the word ‘junkie’ has been applied, the individual disappears and only the label remains. That is not analysis. It is intellectual laziness.

Addiction is not a mysterious condition. It is extensively studied, medically recognised and strongly associated with homelessness, trauma, mental ill-health and social exclusion. National treatment statistics show that among people entering treatment for opiate problems in England in 2024–25, 41 per cent had no home of their own and 10 per cent were sleeping rough. Government research into rough sleeping published in 2025 found that 54 per cent of respondents reported a drug or alcohol misuse need during the preceding year.

These figures do not excuse criminal or antisocial behaviour. They do, however, make a mockery of the idea that addiction can be solved by simply telling somebody to ‘sort themselves out’. A person who is homeless must try to recover without privacy, stability, reliable sleep, secure storage, regular meals or often even basic hygiene. They may need to attend treatment, collect prescriptions, keep appointments, manage benefits, maintain identification documents and navigate housing applications while sleeping outside. To describe failure under those conditions as proof of moral inferiority is not toughness. It is ignorance.

One comment in the local discussion suggested that drug users should do these things ‘behind their own doors’. That statement is revealing precisely because the man in question does not have one.

Most people have the privilege of experiencing their worst behaviour privately. They can drink too much behind curtains, suffer mental-health crises in bedrooms, argue with family in kitchens, withdraw from medication under a duvet or make disastrous decisions without a stranger photographing them. A rough sleeper does not have a private sphere. His bedroom is public. His living room is public. His breakdowns are public. His addiction is public. And then the same society that has left him without a private space condemns him for failing to keep his problems out of sight. There is something deeply incoherent about that.

The man's disability makes the tone of some comments particularly ugly. Government research published in 2025 found that 80 per cent of people surveyed while sleeping rough reported a longstanding physical impairment, illness or disability. Yet a local discussion about a homeless man with one leg included jokes about his wheelchair. There is no serious public-interest argument for that. It is not community safety. It is not concern for children. It is not anger about shoplifting. It is mockery of disability, and adults should be capable of naming that for what it is.

The same applies to language such as ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’. Such terms do not describe conduct; they reduce a person to a social category deemed beneath respect. The implication is that once somebody becomes sufficiently poor, addicted or visibly disordered, ordinary standards of human decency no longer apply to the way we speak about them. That proposition should be rejected. A person's entitlement to dignity cannot depend upon whether they are pleasant enough, clean enough, sober enough or useful enough to satisfy strangers on Facebook.

Rochdale also needs to confront the practical context. The borough is already under intense housing pressure. Under Places for Everyone, Rochdale's housing requirement for 2025 to 2030 is 616 homes per year. Council material from 2025 recorded 7,681 applicants on the housing register, while more recent council reporting has referred to approximately 20,000 people relying upon the register and nearly 7,500 meeting statutory ‘reasonable preference’ criteria. Rochdale Council declared a housing emergency in 2023.

So the instruction often directed at people like this man is effectively the following: become sober, become stable, engage with treatment, organise your paperwork, maintain appointments, secure benefits and compete for scarce housing, all while sleeping outside and managing a major physical disability. That is not impossible. But anyone describing it as simple has probably never attempted anything remotely comparable.

There are also legal considerations when photographs and allegations are published online. Taking a photograph in a public place is not automatically unlawful, and Rochdale Daily is not suggesting otherwise. Identifiable images can, depending on context, constitute personal data, while publishing a photograph alongside a serious allegation of criminal behaviour raises separate legal questions.

The Defamation Act 2013 provides protection against statements that cause or are likely to cause serious reputational harm. Truth may be a defence, but that is different from saying that anything alleged on social media is lawful merely because the publisher believes it. If an identifiable photograph is accompanied by an assertion that a person is committing a criminal offence, the publisher should be in a position to substantiate what is being alleged. Rochdale Daily is therefore not independently stating that the man was consuming a Class A drug based solely on photographs and comments circulated online.

There is an additional point that some contributors may wish to consider before reaching for the camera. Vulnerability does not make somebody public property. The fact that a person's suffering occurs on a pavement does not create an entitlement to turn it into entertainment, gossip or a community spectacle. There may be circumstances in which photographing suspected criminal behaviour serves a legitimate evidential purpose. There is a substantial difference between preserving evidence for police and distributing an image among neighbours so that strangers can compete to produce the most contemptuous description of the person depicted. One is potentially evidence gathering. The other can become a form of public shaming.

And public shaming has a cost. If a person already believes that institutions regard him as worthless, if he already feels humiliated collecting treatment, if strangers photograph him and hundreds of neighbours discuss whether he is a ‘scruff’, then it should not surprise anyone if disengagement, isolation and further drug use follow. People sometimes ask why addicts do not seek help while simultaneously creating a social environment in which admitting addiction results in contempt. They demand recovery while reinforcing shame. They demand engagement while making the person feel despised. They demand that somebody rejoin society while making it clear that society would rather not look at them. Those positions are difficult to reconcile.

There is also a tendency to present compassion as naïveté. Those who have defended the man have been dismissed as ‘Karens’ or ‘do gooders’, as though refusing to join in public degradation demonstrates some failure to understand the realities of addiction. The opposite may be true. It requires very little sophistication to dislike someone behaving badly in public. It requires considerably more maturity to condemn the behaviour without enjoying the destruction of the person.

Compassion does not mean giving unlimited money to somebody with an addiction. It does not mean ignoring theft. It does not mean expecting retail workers to endure abuse. It does not mean pretending crack cocaine is harmless. It means retaining the ability to distinguish a human being from his worst behaviour. That distinction is central to every serious approach to rehabilitation.

If society genuinely wants people to recover from addiction, then those people must eventually be able to imagine themselves as something other than an addict. If every interaction reinforces that they are disgusting, worthless and permanently defined by their dependency, society should not be surprised when they behave as though there is little left to recover.

Rochdale Council lists homelessness support, drug and alcohol treatment and specialist services including Turning Point. Those services are important, but complex cases require coordination. A homeless person with a major physical disability and drug dependency may simultaneously require healthcare, treatment, medication management, benefits assistance, housing support and persistent outreach. That is difficult work. Writing ‘absolute scruff’ beneath a photograph is considerably easier. Perhaps that is part of its appeal. It allows people to experience the satisfaction of condemning a social problem without undertaking any of the difficult work involved in solving it.

There is a legitimate debate to be had about public drug use in Rochdale. There is a legitimate debate about homelessness, shoplifting, antisocial behaviour, policing, treatment capacity and the availability of supported accommodation. Those are serious subjects. Wheelchair jokes are not. Photographing a visibly vulnerable disabled man for the purpose of ridicule is not. Describing somebody at the lowest point of his life as though he were vermin contributes nothing whatsoever to the safety or wellbeing of Rochdale.

Residents are entitled to expect streets that are safe and usable. Tesco staff are entitled to work without abuse. Children should not have to encounter dangerous drug paraphernalia. Police should deal with offences where offences occur. But none of those propositions requires cruelty.

The question for Rochdale is not whether this man is admirable. He may not be. The question is whether a civilised community applies standards of dignity only to people whose lives are already in order. Most of the people commenting about him will eventually put their phones down and return home. They will have a bathroom, a bed, heating, a front door and somewhere to make their mistakes privately. He will still be outside. That difference should produce some humility.

If a community cannot look at a homeless, addicted, disabled man without turning his circumstances into entertainment, then there is more than one social problem on display. One is sitting on the pavement. The other is holding the camera.
